name: Two UML diagrams describe the Composite pattern. Diagram X has boxes Component, Leaf and Composite with operations and generalization arrows. Diagram Y has underlined boxes :Client, two :Composite and six :Leaf, connected by plain lines. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: Diagram X is a class diagram: it describes types, their operations and inheritance.
answers.comment: L1, slide 5: Class boxes with operations and generalization arrows define types, which is what a class diagram shows.

answers.body: Diagram Y is an object diagram: underlined labels with a colon name instances, and the lines are links between them.
answers.comment: L1, slide 5: The underlined "name : Class" notation marks instances, so the right-hand diagram is an object diagram.

answers.body: An object diagram may show several instances of the same class, such as six :Leaf boxes.
answers.comment: L1, slides 5–6: The object diagram contains six :Leaf and two :Composite instances, because one class can have any number of objects.

answers.body: A class diagram contains one box per object that exists at run time.
answers.comment: L1, slide 5: A class diagram describes each type once; individual run-time objects belong in an object diagram.

answers.body: Generalization arrows between instance boxes are the usual way to show inheritance in an object diagram.
answers.comment: L1, slide 5: Inheritance is a relationship between classes; instances are connected only by links, so it is shown in the class diagram.

name: In a Composite pattern, Leaf and Composite inherit from the abstract class Component, and Composite has an association <TT>children</TT> typed as Component. A Client calls Component operations. Which objects can a Composite hold as children?

answers.body: A Leaf instance, since a Component-typed reference accepts any Component subtype.
answers.comment: L1, slide 6: Leaf is a subtype of Component, so a Component-typed child reference can point to a Leaf.

answers.body: Another Composite instance, which may itself hold further children.
answers.comment: L1, slide 6: Composite is also a Component subtype, so composites can be nested; the object diagram shows a nested :Composite.

answers.body: A Client instance that uses the Component interface.
answers.comment: L1, slides 5–6: Client only depends on Component; using a type does not make Client a subtype, so it cannot be a child.

answers.body: Only objects whose class is exactly Component, not instances of any of its subclasses.
answers.comment: L1, slide 6: Subtype objects can be referenced through the supertype; Component is abstract, so the children are in fact Leaf and Composite objects.

name: A team let an LLM generate an application, and it passes all functional acceptance tests. Which conclusions about the remaining challenges are justified?

answers.body: Maintainability is still open: the code must be adaptable for bug fixes and new feature requests.
answers.comment: L1, slide 8: Maintainability, the ability to adapt code for fixes and new requirements, is named as one of the real problems beyond functionality.

answers.body: Qualities such as efficiency, security and reliability still have to be guaranteed separately.
answers.comment: L1, slide 8: Quality means meeting qualitative demands such as efficiency, security and reliability, which functional tests do not establish.

answers.body: Specifying and verifying the code has also become cheap.
answers.comment: L1, slide 8: The slide contrasts cheap code production with specification, verification and maintenance, which remain hard.

answers.body: Passing functional tests shows that design quality is no longer a bottleneck for this project.
answers.comment: L1, slide 8: Design quality is described as the bottleneck now, for agents as much as for humans, regardless of functional success.

name: Why does system decomposition help with both system complexity and changing requirements?

answers.body: Smaller coherent parts can be maintained and their quality assessed independently.
answers.comment: L1, slides 9 and 19: Decomposition applies "divide et impera" so that each part is small enough to maintain and measure on its own.

answers.body: Isolated parts with clear responsibilities and communication protocols keep a change local.
answers.comment: L1, slide 9: Clear responsibilities and protocols limit how far a requirement change spreads.

answers.body: With a large enough LLM context window, decomposition stops being useful.
answers.comment: L1, slide 9: LLM performance degrades as context grows and information can be missed, so agents also need small contexts.

answers.body: A well-decomposed system prevents users from changing their requirements during development.
answers.comment: L1, slide 9: Requirements keep changing; decomposition limits the impact of changes rather than stopping them.

name: A company introduces AI coding agents. Which of its planned activities belong to process management in the sense of the course?

answers.body: Agreeing on how development tasks are carried out and how team members communicate.
answers.comment: L1, slide 11: Process management covers the dynamic "how to do it" side and collaboration standards inside teams.

answers.body: Deciding which instructions, tools and guardrails the agents receive, and how they are supervised.
answers.comment: L1, slide 11: In the AI era, process management includes managing agents and their harness of instructions, tools and guardrails.

answers.body: Choosing the attributes of the Customer class in the domain model of the product.
answers.comment: L1, slides 11 and 27: Class structure is a matter of system decomposition and modeling, not of how the development process runs.

answers.body: Measuring the response time of the finished product against the agreed performance targets.
answers.comment: L1, slides 11 and 13: Response time is a product quality attribute handled by quality assurance, not a development-process rule.

name: A stakeholder-based quality model (presented with ISO/IEC 25010) distinguishes the customer's user experience, the developer's code quality and the manager's long-term view. Which statements fit this model?

answers.body: Testability and understandability are developer-facing qualities that the customer does not see.
answers.comment: L1, slide 13: They are listed under code quality ("it looks good inside"), the invisible engineering view.

answers.body: Maintainability belongs to the long-term view: whether the system will still work and adapt next year.
answers.comment: L1, slide 13: Maintainability is highlighted in the long-term (manager) view, together with adaptability, portability and scalability.

answers.body: If customers see correct and fast behaviour, the internal code quality is thereby also confirmed.
answers.comment: L1, slide 13: Code quality is invisible to the customer, so good visible behaviour says nothing about it.

answers.body: Security and reliability are internal concerns hidden from the customer.
answers.comment: L1, slide 13: Security and reliability are listed under user experience, the part of quality the customer sees.

name: A designer asks an LLM for a system that is highly secure, very fast and easy to port. What should the designer keep in mind?

answers.body: Priorities must be set explicitly, otherwise the LLM silently picks a trade-off between conflicting qualities.
answers.comment: L1, slide 14: LLMs try to satisfy every request, even conflicting ones, and choose a trade-off for you unless you set priorities.

answers.body: Syntactically correct generated code still needs a separate security review, including the suggested packages.
answers.comment: L1, slide 14: Syntax correctness is much higher than the security pass rate, and suggested packages may not exist and can be hijacked.

answers.body: All quality attributes can be maximised at once if the prompt is detailed enough.
answers.comment: L1, slide 14: Quality attributes often conflict; there is no way to optimise all of them at once.

answers.body: An LLM reliably delivers maintainable output, so designer judgement is needed only for functional correctness.
answers.comment: L1, slide 14: LLMs may struggle to deliver maintainable outputs; the insight of an analyst or designer is still required.

name: Which measures improve software quality according to the course?

answers.body: Standardising processes and development tactics, and running regular (automated) tests and code reviews.
answers.comment: L1, slide 15: Standardisation, regular automated testing and code reviews are listed as ways to improve quality.

answers.body: Quality by Design: building quality in through selected patterns, for example by requiring AI agents to use them.
answers.comment: L1, slides 15–16: Patterns are a form of standardisation; forcing agents to use selected patterns is the Quality by Design example.

answers.body: Letting the agents choose patterns freely, with little management or review of their output.
answers.comment: L1, slide 15: LLMs can help with testing and reviews, but only if they are managed properly.

answers.body: Postponing quality decisions until the application is fully implemented and can be measured as a whole.
answers.comment: L1, slides 15–16: Analysis and design patterns address quality during requirements and design, before implementation is finished.

name: Which description matches the mental model of structured (procedural) program execution?

answers.body: Procedures exist in memory before execution, access data segments, and call each other as jumps in code.
answers.comment: L1, slide 18: This is the structured-code model: fixed procedures, shared data segments and calls as jumps.

answers.body: Each procedure instantiates a new object before it may read or write a data segment.
answers.comment: L1, slide 18: Procedures access data segments directly; object instantiation belongs to the OO model.

answers.body: Data and responsibilities are distributed among objects that appear and disappear dynamically.
answers.comment: L1, slides 18 and 22: This describes the object-oriented mental model, not structured code.

answers.body: Calling another procedure changes the data segment but does not transfer control to that procedure.
answers.comment: L1, slide 18: Procedure calls are jumps in code, so they do transfer control.

name: What is a central modeling difficulty of structured decomposition?

answers.body: Functional models (e.g. DFDs) and data models (e.g. ER diagrams) are separate, so both must be kept consistent within and between each other.
answers.comment: L1, slide 20: Structured modeling keeps functional and data models apart, so consistency has to be maintained inside and across them.

answers.body: Functional hierarchies and data clustering remove all relationships between the functional and the data model, so they never need syncing.
answers.comment: L1, slide 21: These techniques organise each model, but the relationships between functional and data models remain too complex.

answers.body: An ER diagram alone captures the functional behaviour, so a separate functional model is redundant.
answers.comment: L1, slide 20: ER diagrams belong to the data model; functions are captured in context and data-flow diagrams.

answers.body: Consistency needs to be checked only inside each individual diagram; the functional and data models describe different aspects and need not agree.
answers.comment: L1, slide 20: The slide names both consistency within models and consistency between models.

name: Which statements match the mental model of object-oriented program execution?

answers.body: Objects cooperate by sending messages: they call other objects' methods and wait for the response.
answers.comment: L1, slide 22: Objects cooperate to respond to a method invocation by calling methods of other objects.

answers.body: Objects can create other objects, and objects appear in and disappear from memory dynamically.
answers.comment: L1, slide 22: Objects can instantiate others, and data and responsibilities live in objects that come and go at run time.

answers.body: Objects are allocated before the program starts, just like procedures in structured code.
answers.comment: L1, slides 18 and 22: Pre-allocation describes procedures in structured code; objects are created dynamically.

answers.body: Objects hold the data, while the responsibilities stay in global procedures that operate on them.
answers.comment: L1, slide 22: Both data and responsibilities are distributed among the objects.

name: What makes an OO decomposition useful for controlling complexity?

answers.body: Tight coupling between data and operations is hidden inside encapsulated parts, while relationships between parts stay loose.
answers.comment: L1, slide 23: Encapsulation hides the internal data-operation coupling, and inter-part relationships should be loosely coupled.

answers.body: Parts can be clustered hierarchically and exist at different granularities, e.g. classes versus components or subsystems.
answers.comment: L1, slide 23: Hierarchical clustering and different granularity are presented as ways to clarify the decomposition.

answers.body: Once the static structure is right, dynamic behaviour needs no further attention or separate modelling.
answers.comment: L1, slide 23: The slide stresses the dynamic behaviour that lies behind the static decomposition.

answers.body: Exposing internal dependencies to the other parts makes the design clearer and easier to change.
answers.comment: L1, slide 23: Dependencies should stay hidden inside parts; many crossing relationships are the situation to avoid.

name: A team uses several OO models (use case, class, interaction and state machine diagrams) and also AI agents. Which practices does the course recommend?

answers.body: Use only the views relevant to the current phase or system part, but check consistency within and between the models used.
answers.comment: L1, slide 24: Not all models are always used, yet life-cycle management and consistency checking inside and between models remain necessary.

answers.body: Treat agent skills and constraints as another form of modeling that controls development.
answers.comment: L1, slide 24: Visual models can be replaced by agent skills and constraints, but that is just another type of modeling and control.

answers.body: Treat the state machine diagram as the main model from which all others are derived.
answers.comment: L1, slide 24: The class diagram is named as the main model, not the state machine diagram.

answers.body: Let the agents generate freely and review only the final result once the whole application runs.
answers.comment: L1, slide 24: Without control, LLMs take the most straightforward solution or over-engineer with needless abstractions and duplicate helpers.

name: LLMs now write most of the code. Which conclusions about the skills a software engineer needs does the course draw?

answers.body: Basic programming knowledge stays valuable: in a cited study it was the dominant predictor of success at LLM-assisted "vibe coding".
answers.comment: L1, slide 25: Success in a basic programming course was the dominant predictor, so introductory courses are not useless.

answers.body: Clear written communication of intent matters, because it directly shapes what the AI produces.
answers.comment: L1, slide 25: Written communication was the second predictor; structuring thoughts in writing affects the generated result.

answers.body: Repository instruction files such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md act as lightweight models that constrain agents.
answers.comment: L1, slide 26: The slide calls these files essentially lightweight models, part of the comeback of model-driven development.

answers.body: Model-driven development is obsolete now that models are no longer useful for guiding code.
answers.comment: L1, slide 26: Model-driven development was suppressed by agile, but it is now making a comeback.

answers.body: Higher-level software engineering principles matter less once nobody writes code by hand.
answers.comment: L1, slide 26: The lecture says the opposite: knowledge of higher-level SE principles becomes even more important.

name: Which pairings of a pattern with its granularity level are correct?

answers.body: Extract Method – low-level refactoring pattern.
answers.comment: L1, slide 32: Extract Method is one of the refactoring examples in the small (low-level) category.

answers.body: Adapter and Composite – middle-level design patterns for class-based models.
answers.comment: L1, slides 27 and 33: GoF design patterns such as Adapter and Composite are middle-level and target maintainable class models.

answers.body: Accounting and Measurement – high-level architectural patterns for whole systems.
answers.comment: L1, slides 27 and 33: These are analysis patterns at the middle level, used to capture functional requirements and the domain.

answers.body: Layers and broker – middle-level design patterns inside one class model.
answers.comment: L1, slide 34: Layers, broker, SOA and peer-to-peer are high-level architectural patterns.

name: Which ideas behind Christopher Alexander's pattern language carry over to software patterns?

answers.body: A pattern describes a problem that recurs in a context, together with the core of its solution.
answers.comment: L1, slide 29: Alexander defines a pattern as the solution of a problem in a given context, for a problem that occurs over and over again.

answers.body: A pattern language documents each pattern's meaning, properties, consequences and relationships, from coarse to fine granularity.
answers.comment: L1, slide 29: Alexander's 253 patterns are well documented and range from coarse-grained to fine-grained.

answers.body: Reusing a pattern means reproducing the same design in each application.
answers.comment: L1, slide 29: The core solution can be used a million times without ever doing it the same way twice.

answers.body: Modern LLM and agentic patterns (e.g. RAG, ReAct) are unrelated to classic patterns and need a completely new theory.
answers.comment: L1, slide 30: The lecture characterises them as largely classic patterns in a new context.

name: What does responsible use of patterns require?

answers.body: Selecting only patterns that serve specific goals, and weighing their consequences when combining them.
answers.comment: L1, slide 31: Only a few patterns are used for specific goals; combined patterns can conflict and have negative consequences.

answers.body: Using pattern names as a shared vocabulary that compresses design intent for both people and agents.
answers.comment: L1, slide 31: "Use a Strategy for pricing rules" packs a whole design intent into a few words that a model understands.

answers.body: Applying as many known patterns as possible to every project to maximise quality.
answers.comment: L1, slide 31: Real projects typically use only a few patterns, chosen for particular goals or parts.

answers.body: Following patterns mechanically wherever possible, without weighing the trade-offs of combining them.
answers.comment: L1, slide 31: Pattern use is a creative process; pattern features can be contradictory.

answers.body: It moves the calculation into a new method, e.g. <TT>computeScore(a, b, c, factor)</TT>, and <TT>foo()</TT> calls it.
answers.comment: L1, slide 32: The example extracts the fragment into computeScore and replaces it with a call.

answers.body: It removes the Long Method and Duplicated Code smells.
answers.comment: L1, slide 32: These two bad smells are listed as the ones solved by Extract Method.

answers.body: It restructures the system into a component architecture such as layers.
answers.comment: L1, slides 32 and 34: Extract Method is a low-level refactoring; layers are a high-level architectural pattern.

answers.body: It removes duplication by copying the calculation into each caller.
answers.comment: L1, slide 32: Copying creates duplication; the refactoring centralises the fragment in one callable method.

answer:
(a) Object diagram. Instances use underlined "name : Class" labels and concrete attribute values; links are plain lines without multiplicities:
object "north : Depot" as north
north : name = "North"
object "south : Depot" as south
south : name = "South"
object "novak : Driver" as novak
novak : name = "Novák"
object "svoboda : Driver" as svoboda
svoboda : name = "Svoboda"
object "t7021 : Vehicle" as t7021
t7021 : number = "7021"
north -- novak
north -- svoboda
north -- t7021
(b) Difference. The class diagram describes types once, with attribute types and multiplicities (1, 0..*). The object diagram shows one particular situation: two Depot objects, two Driver objects and one Vehicle object, with attribute values and links. One class can have many objects (two Depots), and a class can have zero links in a given situation (Depot South), which 0..* allows.
(c) Validity. No. The multiplicity 1 at the Depot end of employs requires every Driver to be linked to exactly one Depot. A Driver without a depot violates the model; if the domain needs such drivers, the multiplicity must become 0..1.
A textual notation like this can be read by both people and LLMs, so it can serve as a shared model.
keyPoints: Object diagram uses instance labels "name : Class", attribute values and links without multiplicities.
Shows two Depot objects, two Driver objects and one Vehicle with exactly the stated links.
Explains that a class diagram describes types and multiplicities, an object diagram one concrete situation.
Notes that Depot South with no links is valid because of 0..*.
Rejects a Driver without a Depot because of multiplicity 1, and names 0..1 as the fix if needed.
source: 01-OO-Fundamentals.pdf, slides 4–5 (textual UML as a shared artifact; class versus object diagram). The depot/driver model is a constructed exercise in the course's transport domain, not taken from a slide.

name:
Read an object diagram given as text. Class model: abstract ModelElement with setColor(Color); Atom and GroupElement inherit from it; GroupElement has association subElements to ModelElement with multiplicity 1..* at the ModelElement end. Instances and links:
g1 : GroupElement  --subElements-->  a1 : Atom
g1 : GroupElement  --subElements-->  g2 : GroupElement
g2 : GroupElement  --subElements-->  a2 : Atom
g2 : GroupElement  --subElements-->  a3 : Atom
a3 : Atom          --subElements-->  a4 : Atom
g3 : GroupElement  (no links)
(a) How many objects of each class are there? (b) Which link or object violates the class model, and why? (c) After removing the illegal link, which Atoms receive setColor when it is called on g1?
answer:
(a) Counts. GroupElement: g1, g2, g3 (3 objects). Atom: a1, a2, a3, a4 (4 objects). No object of ModelElement itself exists, because it is abstract; each object belongs to one concrete class.
(b) Violations.
• The link a3 → a4 is illegal: subElements is defined only on GroupElement, so an Atom has no children.
• g3 violates the multiplicity 1..*: every GroupElement must contain at least one sub-element.
The links g1 → a1, g1 → g2, g2 → a2 and g2 → a3 are legal, because a subElements link can point to any ModelElement subtype, including a nested GroupElement.
(c) Propagation. GroupElement.setColor applies setColor to all children. From g1 the call reaches a1 and g2, and g2 forwards it to a2 and a3. So a1, a2 and a3 get the colour. a4 and g3 are not reachable from g1 (and need fixing anyway).
keyPoints: Counts objects per concrete class: 3 GroupElement, 4 Atom, none of the abstract ModelElement.
Identifies a3 → a4 as illegal because only GroupElement has subElements.
Identifies empty g3 as violating the 1..* multiplicity.
Accepts nested GroupElement children because links may point to any ModelElement subtype.
Traces setColor from g1 to a1, a2 and a3 via g2.
source: 01-OO-Fundamentals.pdf, slides 5–6 and 33 (class and object diagrams; ModelElement/Atom/GroupElement with subElements 1..* and "setColor() is applied to all children"). The instance set is a constructed reading exercise, not copied from a slide.
